message.reasoning: The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want an answer. There's no tool needed. Just respond with a concise answer. Probably mention that lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) share a common ancestor in the order Carnivora? Wait, lions are mammals, specifically within the family Felidae, order Carnivora. Zebras are equids, order Perissodactyla. So their common ancestor would be a more distant mammalian ancestor, perhaps the last common ancestor of all placental mammals, which is the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria? Actually, lions belong to Laurasiatheria (Crown group). Zebras also belong to Laurasiatheria (Perissodactyla). So the common ancestor might be the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria, which is the last common ancestor of all modern mammals that diverged from other mammals. But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species, which is the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae. That would be the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both families, which is the last common ancestor of the clade that includes the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That is the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria. So answer: the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria, which lived around 70 million years ago. Or we can say the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both families, which is the last common ancestor of the clade that includes the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla. So answer: the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria, which existed about 70 million years ago. Provide a concise answer.
